summary: Deprecates the IQUERY operation for inverse DNS lookups from RFC 1035. It was rarely implemented and usually disabled, and pointer records with reverse mapping are the preferred approach. The document tells servers to answer IQUERY requests with a not-implemented error.

plainLanguage.summary: Long ago DNS had a feature to ask what name belongs to this address in a clumsy way. Nobody used it, so this note officially retires it.

questions: what is inverse dns lookup iquery
subtitle: Declaring the DNS IQUERY operation obsolete and no longer recommended

tldr.problem: IQUERY, a DNS operation for inverse lookups defined in RFC 1035, was rarely implemented, usually disabled, and created security and performance risks without providing essential functionality.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC changes the definition of IQUERY opcode 1 from an optional operation to an obsolete one, and recommends that DNS servers return a 'Not Implemented' error when they receive IQUERY requests.
tldr.outcome: Removes an unused feature from the DNS specification, eliminating confusion about whether servers should support it and reducing attack surface.

today: RFC 3425 was published in November 2002 as a Standards Track RFC updating RFC 1035. The IQUERY operation is now officially obsolete. Modern DNS resolvers and servers do not implement IQUERY, and the specification reflects that reality by formally retiring the feature.

sections.title: Background: IQUERY and Its Problems
sections.content:
RFC 1035 defined IQUERY as an inverse DNS operation: instead of looking up a name to find an address, IQUERY looks up an address or other resource record value to find the names associated with it.

However, IQUERY was never widely implemented. Where implementations existed, server operators typically disabled it. The operation creates several problems: a server must either exhaustively search its entire database or maintain a separate reverse-lookup database, both of which strain resources. Response packets can grow to megabyte sizes (for example, returning all domains delegated to a large ISP's nameservers), making the operation vulnerable to denial-of-service attacks. Additionally, IQUERY responses are server-specific and cannot tell a requester where else to look for information.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS had a backward way to ask 'who uses address 1.2.3.4?' But servers found it hard, dangerous, and nobody actually used it.

sections.title: Why IQUERY Is Obsolete
sections.content:
Multiple factors led to obsolescence: IQUERY was optional and never achieved widespread adoption; the only widely deployed reverse-mapping support uses pointer (PTR) records in the in-addr.arpa zone, which proved superior; no known clients rely on IQUERY for any meaningful service; and security concerns motivated operators to disable it.

The RFC notes that response packets from IQUERY could easily be weaponized for denial-of-service attacks. For example, an attacker could probe for all domains under a large provider's control, causing the server to generate an enormous response packet. In the era of early DNSSEC development, IQUERY also created complications because responses would normally need on-the-fly digital signing, which is operationally difficult.
sections.plainLanguage: PTR records do the job better and are everywhere. IQUERY adds nothing valuable but creates performance and security risks.

sections.title: Changes to RFC 1035
sections.content:
This RFC changes the formal definition of IQUERY opcode 1 from an optional operation to one marked as 'obsolete.' The text of RFC 1035 section 6.4, which specified inverse query processing, is now considered obsolete. RFC 3425 provides an updated applicability statement:

Inverse queries using the IQUERY opcode were originally described as the ability to look up the names associated with a particular Resource Record. Their implementation was optional and never achieved widespread use. Therefore IQUERY is now obsolete, and name servers SHOULD return a 'Not Implemented' error when an IQUERY request is received.
sections.plainLanguage: The official book now says this feature is gone. When a server gets an IQUERY request, it should say 'I do not know how to do that.'

sections.title: IANA Considerations and Security
sections.content:
The IQUERY opcode (1) is permanently retired and will not be assigned to any future opcode. This prevents future opcodes from claiming the same number and confusing implementations that remember the old IQUERY definition.

Security implications of obsolescence are minimal: since IQUERY was optional and typically disabled, removing support should not open any security holes. Instead, it reduces the attack surface. If IQUERY had remained in the standard, securing its responses with DNSSEC would have been difficult without on-the-fly signing, which has performance implications.
sections.plainLanguage: The number 1 will never be reused for another operation. Getting rid of IQUERY does not break anything because almost nobody used it.
